body.support:
Every job comes with a **payslip**. It might be paper, an email or an app. Read it!

A payslip is a **text**. Its **purpose** is to show what you earned. Its **audience** is you.

Read it from top to bottom:

1. **Who and when** — your boss's business and the days you're paid for.
2. **Hours × rate** — how many hours, and how much per hour.
3. **Gross pay** — your pay before anything comes out.
4. **Tax** — money sent to the tax office for you.
5. **Net pay** — the money in your bank.
6. **Super** — extra money for later. It goes to your super fund.

You must get a payslip within **one working day** of payday. Something wrong? Check your hours. Then ask your boss, in writing. Still stuck? Call Fair Work.
body.core:
Every job comes with a **payslip**. It might be paper, an email or a page in an app. It's easy to ignore. Don't.

A payslip is a **text**, just like a news article or an ad. It has a **purpose**: to show what you earned and how it was worked out. It has an **audience**: you (and the tax office). And it has a **structure** that's nearly the same everywhere.

Read it from top to bottom:

1. **Who and when** — your employer's name and ABN, your name, the **pay period** (the days it covers) and the **pay date**.
2. **Earnings** — your hours, your **rate** per hour, and the amount. Weekend or late hours may have a higher **penalty rate**.
3. **Gross pay** — the total before anything is taken out.
4. **Deductions** — usually **tax withheld**, which your employer sends to the ATO for you.
5. **Net pay** — what actually goes into your bank.
6. **Super** — extra money your employer pays into your super fund. From 1 July 2025 it's **12%** of your ordinary earnings.

By law, you must get a payslip within **one working day** of payday. If something looks wrong, check your own record of your hours first. Then ask your manager — politely and in writing, so there's a record. If that doesn't fix it, the Fair Work Ombudsman can help.

body.support:
The **Fair Work Ombudsman** checks that workers are paid the right amount.

In one year (2024–25), it got back **$358 million** for more than **249,000** workers who were paid too little.

It said **young workers (15 to 24)** reported problems a lot. Many young people don't check their payslips.

The money came back because people noticed and spoke up.
body.core:
The **Fair Work Ombudsman** is a government body. Its job is to check that workers are paid properly.

In 2024–25, it got back **$358 million** for workers who were paid too little. That money went to more than **249,000** people.

It also said **young workers aged 15 to 24** made more than their share of anonymous reports. Many young people work casual jobs. Many don't know their rights, or don't read their payslips closely.

Most of that money came back because someone noticed a problem and spoke up.
body.extend:
The **Fair Work Ombudsman** is the government body that checks workers are paid properly. In its 2024–25 report, it said it had recovered **$358 million** for more than **249,000** underpaid workers in one year.

It also said **young workers aged 15 to 24** were over-represented in the anonymous reports it received. Young people are more likely to work casual jobs. They are less likely to know their rights or read their payslips closely.

Most of that money came back because someone noticed something was wrong and spoke up.

body.support:
Super is extra money your boss pays for you. It goes into a **super fund**, not your bank. It's for later, but it's **your** money.

From **1 July 2025**, super is **12%**. If you earn $500, your boss pays $60 more into your super.

Your payslip should show your super.
body.core:
Super is money your employer must pay into a super fund for you, on top of your wages. It's for when you're older — but it's still **your** money.

The ATO told employers that from **1 July 2025** the super rate rose to **12%** of your ordinary earnings. If you earn $500 in ordinary pay, your employer pays another $60 into your super.

Your payslip should show how much super was paid and which fund it went to. If it doesn't show up in your fund, ask.
body.extend:
Super is money your employer must pay into a super fund for you, on top of your wages. It's for retirement — but it's legally **your** money.

The ATO told employers that from **1 July 2025** the super guarantee rate rose to **12%** of your ordinary time earnings, applying to all wages paid from that date. If you earn $500 in ordinary pay, your employer pays another $60 into your super.

One catch: if you're **under 18**, your employer only has to pay super for weeks when you work **more than 30 hours**. Your payslip should show super paid and the fund name — and it's worth checking your fund to make sure it actually arrived.

teacher.overview:
Students read a payslip as a **text**: identifying its purpose, audience and structure, annotating its features, and inferring what is missing or wrong. They apply this to real-life scenarios and finish by writing a workplace email to fix a pay error. It's a high-relevance entry point for VM students, many of whom already have casual jobs.

The example payslip is fictional and uses simple round-number rates; it is **not** a guide to actual award rates. Real rates should be checked with the Fair Work Pay Calculator.
prep: If students have jobs, invite them to bring a payslip with personal details covered (optional — never required).
Check the Fair Work Ombudsman pay slips page and Pay Calculator for any changes before teaching.
Have the explainer ready on the board (Watch tab).

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — A payslip is a text
steps: **Hook (5 min):** “You worked 24 hours and got $596. Is that right?” Quick vote.
**Explicit teaching (15 min):** purpose, audience and structure of a payslip. Model reading top to bottom with the example, thinking aloud.
**Watch (5 min):** play the explainer.
**Vocab (10 min):** Word Power page; students use each word about a job they have or want.
**Exit:** name three parts of a payslip and what each tells you.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Annotate and check
steps: **Read (15 min):** “Your payslip is a text”; Check your reading.
**Model (10 min):** annotate markers 1–3 together.
**Independent (25 min):** finish annotating; OK or not OK? sort in pairs.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Real cases and the maths
steps: **Case study (15 min):** the Fair Work Ombudsman report; discuss why young workers are over-represented.
**Do the maths (15 min):** model the first row; students check the rest.
**Scenarios (20 min):** Check. Ask. Get help.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Write the email
steps: **Model (10 min):** write a weak and a strong email on the board; compare tone and structure.
**Write (25 min):** final mission. Fast finishers: Level Up challenge.
**Check & reflect (15 min):** quick check on the app, reflection, request sign-off.

keyPoints: A payslip has a purpose (show earnings), an audience (the worker) and a predictable structure.
Gross − deductions = net. Super is extra and goes to the fund, not the bank.
Payslips must be given within one working day of payday.
Check → Ask (in writing) → Get help (Fair Work Ombudsman, 13 13 94).

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** purpose = show what you earned and how it was worked out; audience = the worker (and the ATO); gross = before deductions, net = what you take home; in writing = there's a record.

**Read the payslip:** 1 employer and ABN; 2 pay period and pay date; 3 hours × rate (earnings); 4 gross pay; 5 tax withheld; 6 net pay; 7 super paid to the fund.

**OK or not OK?** Friday payslip — OK. Three weeks, none — Not OK. 15 vs 19 hours — Not OK. Net less than gross — OK. No super at 19 — Ask (should be paid). App payslip — OK.

**Do the maths:** Saturday 6 × $30 = $180; gross $432 + $180 = $612; net $612 − $16 = $596; super 12% × $612 = $73.44.
